Stealth technology in the U.S. military began focused research in the early 1950s at the Air Force Avionics Laboratory.
Radar Cross Section (RCS) varies wildly with aspect angle, sometimes by factors of 1000 or more within small angular spans.
Radar signal strength returning from a target decreases with the fourth power of the target range.
A 95% reduction in radar signature reduces radar detection range by 50%, while a 99% reduction reduces it by 67%.
Dynamic RCS measurements on flying aircraft are limited by instrumentation complexity and difficulty in knowing exact aspect angles.
Model measurements in anechoic chambers became the preferred method for RCS characterization due to better control and repeatability.
Anechoic chambers require special absorber materials and low-echo supports to minimize background reflections during RCS testing.
Early RCS models required high detail; gross geometry alone produced erroneous results.
Radar absorber materials (RAM) development started in 1955 to reduce radar signatures by absorbing radar energy.
RAM must be thin, lightweight, durable under flight conditions, and maintain smooth aerodynamic surfaces.
Impulse measurement techniques were developed to characterize RAM electrical properties over a wide frequency range quickly and accurately.
A T-33 aircraft was fully coated with broadband RAM and successfully flown to demonstrate real-world stealth material performance.
Radar echo patterns show complex lobe structures caused by interference from different aircraft surfaces.
Blending with the radar background is easier for ground vehicles due to clutter; airborne vehicles face near-zero radar background, requiring more stringent stealth.
Cost-effectiveness is a key consideration in how much radar signature reduction is pursued, as zero signature is impractical.
Metal screens with fine mesh can behave like solid metal to radar, affecting engine inlet radar signatures.
Early computational methods for RCS were limited by available computing power and complexity of aircraft shapes.
The Air Force Avionics Laboratory developed a specialized large anechoic chamber known as 'the barn' for RCS testing.
Radar frequency affects whether an aircraft's radar echo behaves as multiple discrete sources or as a single large source.
Flight tests with RAM-covered aircraft validated laboratory model predictions of radar signature reduction.
